trophies.name: Vice Got a Price!
strategy: Treat this trophy as a receipt, not a target: it unlocks by itself the moment the other fifty-four trophies are all on your account, so every hour of the hunt is aimed at them, never at this one directly.

Keep your tracker truthful as you go. Tick each trophy on the day it pops and, once per roadmap phase, compare the count on this page against the PlayStation trophy screen so nothing earned quietly is ever hunted twice.

Guard the hunt's two fragile points — the story choice behind Actions Speak Louder and the fail-first moment behind Bad Luck, I Guess — with the chapter-break saves from the rules, and the rest of the list can never be lost.

In the endgame, work only from the in-game stats and 100% checklist screens. They count stunts, cards, spots, challenges and money exactly; the distance between those numbers and the targets is your real remaining work.

When the fifty-fourth trophy lands, stay somewhere scenic for a few seconds. The platinum follows automatically, there is nothing to press or claim, and you have earned the right to watch this one arrive.
trophies.tip: It awards itself — earn the other 54 and the platinum is the receipt.

trophies.name: Just Like Paradise
strategy: This is the campaign's gentle on-ramp: Gone Fishing is an early story mission that doubles as the game's fishing tutorial, and it cannot be skipped or failed permanently, so simply play the opening until it arrives.

Follow the mission markers to the water and do what the prompts teach — cast, watch the float, reel against the fish's runs rather than against the line's tension. The mission is generous with retries inside each step.

If a catch escapes, treat it as the lesson the mission intends: ease off the reel while the fish is running and recover line while it rests. Two or three attempts at most will teach the rhythm the whole fishing system uses.
Finish the mission's closing conversation instead of wandering off mid-beat; story trophies register on completion, and the pop lands as the mission wraps and control returns to you in free roam.

Before you move on, make the hunt's first habit: a manual save in a fresh slot. Gone Fishing sits early enough that this save also anchors your chapter-break collection for the two missable trophies later.
trophies.tip: Play the opening story — this one is the fishing tutorial and pops on completion.

trophies.name: Paradise Lost
strategy: Chapter 1 is the whole introduction: Lucia, Jason, the first stretch of Vice City and every core system in miniature. There is no way to miss this trophy — it pays for finishing the chapter, however you choose to play it.

Resist the open world's pull for these first hours. Side icons will accumulate, but the chapter's missions unlock the map, the garages and the systems the later phases need, so the campaign is the fastest route to everything.

Use the chapter to learn cheap lessons: how wanted levels rise and cool, how the two protagonists swap, where the nearest save and health are. Nothing here is scored, so experiment while experimentation is free.

Start two habits now that the grind phase will thank you for: register any new vehicle you drive to the Scooter Bros app, and glance at the stats screen after each session so the long counters never surprise you.

When the chapter's final mission closes, the trophy pops and your first chapter-break save should go into its own slot. That save is the template for the save discipline the two missable trophies depend on.
trophies.tip: Finish Chapter 1 — unmissable, and it unlocks the systems the whole hunt uses.

trophies.name: T**s Ass Drug Money
strategy: Chapter 2 widens the story into Leonida's money economy — the deals, fronts and laundering that several economy trophies later formalise. Like every chapter trophy it is unmissable: finish the chapter's missions and it pays.

By now stranger markers begin appearing between missions. Open each strand the moment you see it, even if you drive straight back to the story afterwards; strands ripen on in-game days and early opening is free progress.

Marked Bills start flowing through your hands in this chapter. Whenever the game offers a laundering contact, use it — the $250,000 laundering counter behind Dime on the Dollar is painless only if it starts here.

Keep the save discipline from Chapter 1: one fresh slot at the chapter break, never overwritten. The missable story choice is still ahead of you, and these boring saves are precisely what makes it safe.

Expect the difficulty to step up gently — longer drives, busier shootouts. Restock ammunition and armour between missions rather than during them, and the chapter's set pieces stay comfortable from start to finish.
trophies.tip: Finish Chapter 2, launder Marked Bills whenever offered, and bank the chapter-break save.

trophies.name: Vice City, Baby!
strategy: Chapter 3 is the Vice City chapter — the neon core of the map opens fully and the story settles into the city that gives the trophy its name. It is unmissable: the trophy pays when the chapter's last mission closes.

The city's density makes this the natural moment to begin the exploration habits: drive new vehicles rather than the same favourite, register them to Scooter Bros, and let the 100-vehicle discovery counter grow in the background.

Ocean Beach and the beachfront strip feature heavily here. While you are in the neighbourhood, the cocktail-with-a-view spot behind In The Beginning… is a two-minute detour you will otherwise make a special trip for later.

Stranger strands multiply in the city. Keep opening them on sight and let their pauses overlap the story; by the chapter's end you should have every early strand running, which sets up the whole of Phase 2.

Close the chapter, take the trophy, and write your chapter-break save before doing anything else. Three chapters of save discipline should now be automatic — the missable moments are close enough to matter.
trophies.tip: Finish Chapter 3 — sweep Ocean Beach while the story has you there anyway.

trophies.name: Top Of The World, Ma
strategy: Chapter 4 pushes the story out of the city and up in the world — Mount Kalaga and the northern map feature as the stakes climb. The trophy is the usual chapter deal: unmissable, paid in full when the final mission ends.

The northern districts are the map's emptiest, so fold exploration into the story drives: meditation spots and stunt locations sit near these roads, and a ten-minute detour now saves a dedicated expedition in Phase 4.

Money should be healthy by this chapter. Resist splurging it all on cars — the garage-property trophy later wants serious capital, and Treat Yo Self only asks for $100,000 spent across the whole game, which happens naturally.

If any strand has gone quiet, check its marker before starting the chapter's point-of-no-return mission; long story sequences can delay strand timers, and a strand checked now is a strand that keeps ripening.

Finish the chapter and protect the moment with the usual fresh save. You are past halfway through the campaign, and from here the roadmap's remaining story trophies are individual missions rather than whole chapters.
trophies.tip: Finish Chapter 4 — detour to northern meditation and stunt spots while the story drives you there.

trophies.name: You Gotta Know When to Get Off
strategy: The gold is for the campaign's final mission, and it is unmissable in the only sense that matters: starting it with a save outside means a failed attempt costs minutes, so make that save before you accept the mission.

Prepare like it is a heist, because structurally it is one: full health and armour, every weapon stocked, a fast car you trust parked where the mission begins. The finale chains its set pieces without shopping breaks.

Play the long middle sections patiently. Finale missions in this series spike when players rush cover to cover; move when fire slackens, use Combat Focus for crowded rooms, and let your partner's fire do quiet work.

One story choice on the road here carries the missable Actions Speak Louder trophy. If you kept chapter-break saves you can always return for the other outcome, so choose the one that fits your Lucia and Jason without anxiety.

When the credits finish, do not start hunting immediately. Save once in free roam — this becomes your post-story anchor — then check the stats screen: the story's twelve trophies are done, and the counters show the true size of what remains.
trophies.tip: Save before the finale, stock up like a heist, and the gold is yours at the credits.

trophies.name: Trust
strategy: Breakfast Run is a short, warm story mission built around the two protagonists learning to rely on each other, and the trophy simply asks you to finish it. It arrives early and cannot be missed or failed for good.

Play it as the game intends the first time: follow the route, listen to the conversation, and let the mission teach you how the pair hand tasks between themselves, because later partner trophies reuse exactly these mechanics.

Any driving or chase beat that goes wrong is checkpointed generously. If you spin out or lose the trail, the mission restarts you seconds back rather than at the start, so push on instead of reloading a save.

The trophy registers when the mission wraps, not during its final drive. Stay through the closing scene until control returns and the completion banner has had its moment, then check it off in the tracker.

Because it is quick, this mission is a good early test of your setup habits: save before and after it, and you will have rehearsed the routine that protects the genuinely missable moments much later in the story.
trophies.tip: Finish Breakfast Run — a short early mission with generous checkpoints.

trophies.name: Break the Bank
strategy: The Cartel Heist is the campaign's first full heist and the template for every robbery trophy after it. The trophy needs completion only — no score, no gold medal, no minimum take — so survive it first and optimise never.

In the setup beats, actually do the scouting the mission offers. The entry points, guard rhythms and exit streets it shows you are the same knowledge the combat phase of this guide assumes you have practised here.

During the escape, remember the hunt rule: the getaway was planned before the grab. Follow the route the mission lays out rather than improvising across town, and swap vehicles when the mission suggests it instead of clinging to a burning car.

Combat Focus is your pressure valve in the vault and yard fights. Save it for the moments when enemies arrive from two sides at once; a single well-timed use clears the room that would otherwise cost a checkpoint.

When the take is split and the heat dies, the trophy pops. Note what the heist taught you — bank vaults in free roam, behind Maximum Withdrawal, run on this same skeleton with the training wheels removed.
trophies.tip: Complete The Cartel Heist — completion only, so scout well and follow the planned escape.

trophies.name: Family Matters
strategy: Child's Play is a character-first story mission — quieter than the heists around it, with its difficulty in driving and timing beats rather than gunfights. Finish it and the trophy is yours; nothing about it can be missed.

Slow down for its set pieces. Missions built around family and errands tend to fail players who treat them like races; the timers here are padded, and the checkpoints forgive the occasional wrong turn or missed marker.

Listen to the dialogue rather than skipping it. This mission plants relationships and locations that later strands and story beats reuse, and knowing who people are makes several Phase 2 strands easier to follow and faster to finish.

If a vehicle section frustrates, switch to a sturdier car at the next opportunity the mission allows. The mission cares that you arrive, not what you arrive in, and armour on wheels is a legitimate strategy throughout this guide.

As the mission closes, keep the routine: trophy, fresh save, quick stats glance. Child's Play usually lands mid-chapter, so it is also a natural moment to open any stranger strand whose marker appeared nearby.
trophies.tip: Finish Child's Play — take it gently; the timers are padded and checkpoints kind.

trophies.name: DWNFALL
strategy: Headliners is the story's nightclub-and-headlines mission, a mid-campaign set piece mixing driving, crowd scenes and a loud finale. The trophy pays on completion, and like all named-mission trophies it cannot be missed.

Expect the mission to move between on-foot and vehicle beats quickly. Keep a balanced loadout rather than specialising: a reliable automatic, something with range, and full armour will cover every phase it throws at you.

In crowd and venue sections, move with purpose but do not sprint blindly — bumping through crowds and clipping scenery costs more time than a steady line, and the mission's timers assume a calm player, not a perfect one.

The finale's escape is a rehearsal for the free-roam robbery trophies: break line of sight first, then change direction, then let the wanted level cool somewhere quiet instead of racing the stars across the whole city.

After the completion banner, you will likely be near venues and activities the map has been teasing. Finish the save-and-tick routine first, then let Phase 3 curiosity have the next half hour — you have earned it.
trophies.tip: Finish Headliners — balanced loadout, calm lines through crowds, planned escape at the end.

trophies.name: Hi-Jacked
strategy: VCIA Takedown takes the story to Vice City International Airport, and its trophy pays on completion. The airport will matter again later — Catch Me If You Can happens here — so treat this mission as a guided tour of a future playground.

Learn the airport's geometry while the mission shows it to you: the terminal frontage, the service roads, the runway access points and the fences that do and do not break. That mental map is worth real minutes in the combat phase.

Vehicle beats at the airport reward nerve over speed. Hold your line on the service roads, use the wide aprons to turn, and do not chase targets across active runways when a parallel road gets you there a second later and alive.

If the mission asks for a departure or a theft under pressure, commit fully once you start. Half-hearted attempts keep you in the open under fire; a decisive run at the objective shortens every dangerous section of this mission.

When the takedown wraps and the trophy lands, note the airport's exits on your mental map before you leave. You will be back here to make an unscheduled departure, and arriving already oriented is the whole trick.
trophies.tip: Finish VCIA Takedown — and memorise the airport layout; you will need it again.

trophies.name: Snow Storm
strategy: Operation Savage Glory is one of the campaign's bigger military-flavoured operations — a longer mission with staged assaults and vehicle sections. Completion is all the trophy asks, and the mission's checkpoints are placed like a fair editor's.

Go in heavy and stay heavy: full armour, full ammunition for two weapon classes, and snacks or health items where the game allows them. Long operations punish the player who has to scavenge mid-fight far more than the slow one.

Advance in bounds. Each staged fight has a piece of cover that commands it; take that cover, clear the wave, then move. Rushing to the objective marker through live fire is the single most common way this mission eats retries.

Vehicle sections between the assaults are breathers by design. Use them to let health recover and to re-orient on the map — the operation covers ground, and arriving at each stage knowing which way is out is quiet, real preparation.

The trophy pops as the operation concludes. This is usually a late-campaign mission, so afterwards take stock: the finale is close, your chapter saves should be complete, and the two missable moments deserve one last thought before you proceed.
trophies.tip: Finish Operation Savage Glory — bound from cover to cover and arrive stocked.

trophies.name: A Long Road
strategy: This gold answers to the game's own 100% checklist, not to this guide's list — the two overlap heavily but are not identical, so from mid-game onwards the checklist screen in the game is the document you are actually completing.

Open the checklist once per phase and clear its cheapest missing lines first. Completion percentages hide lumps: a strand instalment or a single activity type can be worth more than an hour of counter-grinding, and the screen tells you exactly where the lumps are.

The usual final gaps are unglamorous: one strand not quite finished, one activity type tried but not completed, a collectible category a few short. Work the checklist top to bottom in one sitting rather than guessing from memory.

Beware the difference between discovered and completed. Several checklist lines require finishing the thing — the race, the strand, the challenge — not merely starting it, which is why the tracker on this page separates tried from earned in spirit.

When the screen finally reads 100%, the gold pays immediately. What remains for the platinum is only trophies, not completion — compare the two lists, hunt any trophy the checklist did not cover, and Vice Got a Price! closes the hunt.
trophies.tip: The in-game checklist is the real document — clear its cheapest missing lines first.

trophies.name: Cunning Stunts
strategy: Two hundred and fifty stunts sounds like a wall until you price it honestly: at roughly ninety seconds per attempt including the drive between ramps, it is six to ten hours — but only if you start during the story, as the hunt rules insist.

Learn what the game counts. A stunt registers when the jump, flip or spin lands cleanly and the on-screen stunt banner confirms it; a crashed landing that felt spectacular counts for nothing, so chase clean landings, not height.

Build three or four short circuits in districts you visit often — Vice City rooftops and ramps, the Keys causeways, the Kalaga switchbacks — and run a circuit whenever a session starts nearby. Five stunts a session, every session, finishes this without a single dedicated grind day.

Use the right tools: a light sports bike for ramp work, a nimble car for rooftop gaps, and a fresh vehicle after every hard landing. Wrecked suspension quietly ruins stunt attempts long before the vehicle looks damaged.

Track the counter on the stats screen, never from memory, and when the last fifty remain, dedicate one session to your fastest circuit on repeat. The silver pays at 250 confirmed stunts — the banner, not the attempt, is the unit.
trophies.tip: Five clean stunts a session from Chapter 1 onwards, and 250 arrives by itself.

trophies.name: Master of None
trophies.description: Try each type of activity once.
strategy: The friendliest trophy on the list: the game only asks that you try each type of activity once — not win it, not finish it well, just show up and take part. One deliberate lap of the activity icons earns it in an afternoon.

Open the map and filter to activities, then plan a route that strings the types together geographically instead of teleporting between them. Driving the route yourself also feeds vehicle discovery and map exploration, so the lap pays three times.

At each stop, actually start the activity and play its opening minute. Walking up to a marker is not a try; the counter moves when the activity begins, and most types confirm with their own little banner or results screen.

Keep a note of which types you enjoyed, because the lap doubles as reconnaissance: the range, the drone races and the race series all have their own trophies later, and knowing your favourites now makes Phase 3 planning trivial.

If the trophy has not popped after your lap, one type is still untried — usually the one whose icon hides inside another venue, like the arcade machines or the bowling alley. Sweep the map filter once more and the missing type announces itself.
trophies.tip: One lap of the activity icons, starting each one properly — trying is all it asks.

trophies.name: The Shootist
trophies.description: Earn a gold medal in all Shooting Range challenges.
strategy: Gold at every shooting-range challenge is the list's purest skill test, and it is still mostly a preparation test: medals are scored on accuracy and streaks, so the winning skill is a calm trigger, not a fast one.

Learn each challenge's shape before chasing its medal. Run it once slowly to see where targets appear, which are worth bonus points and where the streak breaks hide; a reconnaissance run is never wasted, because the layouts do not change.

Shoot in controlled pairs and let misses go. Chasing a missed target with three wild shots destroys the accuracy figure the medal is built on; the next target is always worth more than revenge on the last one.

Work the challenges in order of difficulty for you, not the menu's order, and bank golds while fresh. When one challenge resists, leave it for a day — range golds fall to rested hands, and tilting at a target pattern only engraves bad habits.

For the final stubborn challenges, slow your aim deliberately below your instinct. Most near-misses at gold are speed errors in the last third of a run, when the medal feels close; a boring, steady finish beats a heroic one every time.
trophies.tip: Recon each layout once, shoot in calm pairs, and never chase a missed target.

trophies.name: Top Fun
trophies.description: Win a Top Fun Drone Race at every location.
strategy: Top Fun puts you on a drone against the clock and the course, and the trophy wants a win at every location — not a perfect season, just first place once per site. Learn courses individually; each has its own two or three decisive gates.

Fly the course once at cruising speed before racing it. Drone courses hide their difficulty in vertical moves — a gate above a rooftop, a drop through a structure — and knowing the altitude changes in advance is worth more than any reflex.

Race the line, not the drone ahead. Chasing a rival's tail makes you copy their mistakes; the winning run is the smooth one that clips every gate's centre and never has to double back, because a missed gate costs more than any straight-line speed gains.

Small inputs. Drones punish yanks: roll gently into turns, set your height early for each gate, and treat the throttle like a dimmer rather than a switch. If the drone offers a sensitivity or assist setting, tune it once and then leave it alone.

Keep a simple list of locations won and revisit the stubborn ones fresh rather than in a rage streak. In practice two or three sites hold most of the difficulty, and both usually fall to one calm, memorised run each.
trophies.tip: Scout each course once at cruise speed — smooth lines and centred gates win drone races.

trophies.name: Earn Cash, Not Kudos
strategy: Twenty different races, won — the word different is the trap. Repeating your favourite circuit twenty times earns you money and practice but moves this counter once, so keep a written list of the races you have actually won.

Start with the short point-to-point races in districts you know. Early wins come cheap on familiar roads, and each win teaches the game's racing line — braking markers, traffic behaviour, where the AI drivers are brave and where they hesitate.

Bring the right vehicle class and keep it maintained. Races are lost in the garage as often as on the road: a tuned, repaired car in the correct class beats a heroic drive in the wrong one, and upgrades bought here also serve the exploration phases.

Race clean for the first half and defend in the second. The pack is fastest to pass in the opening corners while it is bunched; once you lead, your job is an untroubled line and no unforced meetings with lampposts, because one spin usually ends a win.

If a particular race resists, change the conditions before changing yourself: a different vehicle in class, a retry at a quieter in-game hour, or simply later, when your map knowledge has grown. Twenty wins across a whole state is a tour, not a wall.
trophies.tip: Keep a list — it must be 20 different races, and repeats only count once.

trophies.name: Baited My Tackle
trophies.description: Beat Cal in a fishing challenge.
strategy: Cal is the game's fishing rival, and his challenge is a fair duel under the same rules Gone Fishing taught you: cast well, read the water, and land your catches without snapping the line. Beat his total and the trophy is yours.

Practise on free fishing first if the story mission is a distant memory. Ten minutes of unpressured casts restores the rhythm — let the fish run, reel while it rests — and reminds you how the tension gauge behaves before it costs you a duel.

In the challenge itself, fish for consistency over glory. A string of medium catches landed beats one monster lost at the bank; every snapped line is time spent re-rigging while Cal's total keeps climbing on fish you could have banked.

Watch where Cal casts and what he catches. The game is quietly teaching you where the fish are: if his float is finding bites in a spot and yours is silent, move. There is no prize for loyalty to unproductive water.

If you lose a round, challenge him again immediately while the spot and the rhythm are fresh — fishing challenges are short, and most players take him on the second or third attempt once the tension discipline from the first loss has sunk in.
trophies.tip: Land everything, chase nothing huge — consistency beats Cal, heroics snap lines.

trophies.name: Stick Fiddler
strategy: Somewhere in Leonida an arcade cabinet is waiting to be the easiest bronze on the list: the trophy asks you to complete an arcade game — play one through to its end or completion screen, not merely to insert a coin and wander off.

Find a machine during your Master of None lap, because arcades are one of the activity types players most often walk past. Bars, arcades and entertainment venues on the beachfront and in the city are the natural places to look.

Choose the shortest game on offer if the cabinet gives you a menu. Completion is completion: the trophy does not grade which cabinet classic you finished, so a five-minute game earns exactly the same bronze as a half-hour one.

If the game has lives or continues, use them without pride. Arcade design assumes repeated attempts, and the completion the trophy wants is reaching the end screen by whatever honest route the machine itself offers.

Once the completion screen shows and the trophy lands, you have also banked one of the easiest activity types for the Master of None counter — two birds, one cabinet, and a story to tell about the platinum hunt's gentlest hour.
trophies.tip: Pick the shortest cabinet game and play it to its end screen — that is the whole trophy.

trophies.name: Road to Rehabilitation
trophies.description: Complete the final mission for Andy.
strategy: Andy's strand is a recovery story told in instalments, and this trophy pays when its final mission is complete. The strand's real requirement is calendar, not skill: instalments unlock as in-game days pass, so start it early.

Open the strand the first time Andy's marker appears, even if you are mid-chapter. Each meeting is short; the waiting between them is the long part, and waiting started in Chapter 2 finishes long before the endgame needs it done.

Between instalments, advance time honestly: play other content, sleep at a safehouse, live the game. Strands check their timers as days roll over, and a strand checked once per session never becomes the bottleneck it becomes when ignored for weeks.

Andy's later missions ask a little more of you — escorts, pickups, small favours under mild pressure. None of it is scored, so take the sturdy vehicle, drive like you have a passenger you like, and let the story do the heavy lifting.

The final mission closes the strand and pays the trophy on completion. It also counts toward the eight completions Strangers & Freaks wants, so tick both in the tracker: this page's counter and your mental one should always agree.
trophies.tip: Open Andy's strand early — its timer is in-game days, and waiting is the only cost.

trophies.name: This Was No Boat Accident
trophies.description: Complete the final mission for Kenton.
strategy: Kenton's strand smells of salt water and bad decisions, and its trophy pays at the strand's final mission. Like every strand it unfolds in instalments separated by in-game days, so the winning move is simply to start it early.

Expect boats. At least part of this strand lives on the water around the Keys and the coast, so brush up on boat handling in calm conditions first: throttle in the turns, respect the swell, and remember that a slow arrival beats a beached one.

When the strand asks you to find, fetch or investigate around the shoreline, work the coast methodically rather than swimming at markers. Most strand objectives sit near docks, ramps and moorings — the places a boat person would actually be.

Keep the strand moving between story chapters. Kenton's pauses overlap the campaign perfectly if you check the marker once per session; left alone until the endgame, the same strand feels like it is deliberately wasting your evenings.

Finish the final mission and the trophy pays, along with another completion toward Strangers & Freaks. If the strand's title made you glance at the water differently, the writers did their job — it was, in fact, no boat accident.
trophies.tip: Start Kenton early and practise boat handling in calm water before his strand needs it.

trophies.name: The Lone Rider
trophies.description: Complete the final mission for Billy.
strategy: Billy rides alone and his strand is built around the road — long drives, open country and the Leonida beyond the city lights. The trophy pays at his final mission, reached through instalments that unlock as in-game days pass.

Open the strand as soon as Billy's marker appears and let it ripen alongside the campaign. His meetings tend to sit far from Vice City, so fold each visit into a trip you are already making — an exploration sweep, a northern chapter drive.

Bring a bike you trust for his missions, or at least arrive on wheels that suit the country. Strand missions often start where you meet the character; showing up in the wrong vehicle costs a long walk to something suitable.

The drives in this strand are the point, not the padding. Use them: stunt ramps, meditation spots and undiscovered vehicles all live along these rural routes, and a Billy trip run properly pays into three other counters on the way.

Complete the final mission and the bronze lands, with another strand completion banked for Strangers & Freaks. Billy's story ends the way it ran — on the road — and your strand count should now be visibly climbing.
trophies.tip: Fold Billy's far-flung meetings into trips you are already making across the north.

trophies.name: Strangers & Freaks
trophies.description: Complete 8 mission strands for strangers across the state of Leonida.
strategy: The silver wants eight stranger strands completed across the state — more than the five named strand trophies, so you will finish strands this guide has no separate bronze for. The system is the strategy: open everything, finish everything.

Strands are timers wearing stories. Each advances in instalments separated by in-game days, so your real resource is elapsed calendar: a strand opened in the first week finishes in the background, while one opened at the endgame makes you wait in real time.

Keep a strand ledger — in this tracker or on paper — noting whose strand is open, whose is ripening and whose final mission is ready. Two minutes of bookkeeping per session prevents the classic failure: seven strands at 90% and no idea which is which.

When several final missions are ready, close them in one geographic sweep. Strand finales cluster your travel; a single evening's drive around Leonida can convert three ripe strands into three completions and most of this silver in one motion.

If you reach the endgame a strand short, the map is not empty — it is unfiltered. Re-check the stranger markers in districts you rushed during the story; the eighth strand is almost always one you opened, enjoyed, and forgot to revisit.
trophies.tip: Open every strand early and keep a ledger — eight completions is a calendar game.

trophies.name: Supply & Demand
trophies.description: Complete the final mission for Randy.
strategy: Randy deals in goods that need moving, and his strand is a small logistics business disguised as a story: pickups, deliveries and the occasional complication. The trophy pays at the final mission, after the usual instalments and in-game days.

Start the strand early like all the others, and drive Randy's jobs in vehicles with room and armour. Deliveries that arrive are worth more than deliveries that arrive fast; the strand never scores your style, only your completion.

Learn Randy's patch of Leonida as you work. His pickups and drop-offs sketch a little economy of warehouses, yards and back lots, and that local knowledge quietly serves the later robbery and gang-operation trophies in the same districts.

When a delivery goes loud — and one always does — remember the escape rule from the hunt rules: break line of sight, change direction once, then cool down somewhere boring. Randy will still be there when the stars are gone.

The final mission closes Randy's books and pays the trophy, plus one more completion toward Strangers & Freaks. By now the strand rhythm should be second nature: open early, check often, close them in geographic sweeps.
trophies.tip: Drive Randy's deliveries in something roomy and armoured — arriving matters, speed does not.

trophies.name: Spin On This!
trophies.description: Complete the final mission for Tyrone.
strategy: Tyrone's strand spins around wheels and showing off, and its trophy pays at the final mission after the usual chain of instalments. Start it the moment the marker appears; strands are calendar creatures and this one is no exception.

Expect driving with flair. Tyrone's world cares about how things look, so his missions lean toward vehicle tricks and proud arrivals — the same skills your stunt counter is quietly building, which makes his instalments unusually productive time.

Keep a stunt-capable car or bike as your daily driver while his strand is active. You will pass ramps and gaps on the way to his markers anyway; arriving via a clean stunt or two turns strand travel into Cunning Stunts progress at no extra cost.

Check the marker once per session and let the pauses overlap the campaign. Tyrone's strand, like the other five, only becomes a chore if it is saved for the endgame and its waiting has nowhere left to hide.

Finish the final mission and both the bronze and another Strangers & Freaks completion are yours. Five named strands down — the silver's remaining completions come from the strands beyond the named five, so keep opening markers.
trophies.tip: Run Tyrone's errands in a stunt-capable ride and let his travel feed the stunt counter.

trophies.name: Positive Mental Attitude
trophies.description: Meditate at every spot across Leonida.
strategy: Scattered across Leonida are meditation spots — quiet viewpoints, summits, shorelines — and this trophy asks you to meditate at every single one. It is the hunt's most peaceful counter and one of its easiest to complete early.

Spots sit where the view earns it: Mount Kalaga's heights, Keys causeways, Grassrivers clearings, beach ends at dawn. When you reach one, the interaction is unhurried — stand where prompted, let the meditation play out fully, and only move on once it registers.

Sweep region by region rather than criss-crossing the state. Combine each region's spots with whatever else that region holds — strands, stunts, vehicles — and the meditation tour becomes the skeleton of your whole exploration phase.

Keep count from the stats or checklist screen rather than from a list of your own. The classic failure here is the spot you visited, admired and left a second too early; if your total is one short at the end, it is that spot, wherever it was.

Do the last sweep in one sitting with fresh eyes if the counter stalls. Meditation spots reward slowness in finding as well as in use: they are placed to be noticed by a player who has stopped hurrying, which is presumably the point.
trophies.tip: Sweep region by region and let each meditation fully register before you walk away.

trophies.name: Fair Game
trophies.description: Hunt a unique animal for Bret.
strategy: Bret wants a unique animal — not any deer in the Grassrivers, but a specific, named-calibre quarry, and this trophy pays when you hunt it for him. Treat it as a small detective story: learn the animal, find its ground, then make the hunt itself the easy part.

Take Bret's briefing seriously. Strand-givers in this series describe their quarry precisely — habitat, habits, signs — and the unique animal will be where the description says it lives, at the times such an animal would move. The briefing is the map.

Prepare like a hunter, not a tourist: a suitable long-range weapon, patience, and an approach from downwind or cover where the game models it. Unique animals spook like ordinary ones, only there is exactly one of them to spook.

If the hunt fails — the animal bolts, the trail goes cold — do not chase it across the county. Return to Bret's starting point or reload the area and begin the stalk again; scripted hunts reset their quarry, and a fresh, quiet approach beats a desperate pursuit.

When the animal is down and Bret's requirement is met, the trophy pays. The skills are transferable: the same patience and ground-reading serve the exploration phase's quieter corners, and the Grassrivers will feel smaller ever after.
trophies.tip: Bret's briefing is the map — hunt where and when the description says the animal lives.

trophies.name: Don't Touch My Deck
strategy: Collectible cards hide across Leonida in themed sets, and the silver wants three complete sets — not three cards, three finished collections. The good news is that sets are completable one at a time; the discipline is knowing which set each found card belongs to.

Pick your three sets deliberately once you have seen the categories: choose sets whose cards cluster in districts you already sweep for other work. A set spread across the Grassrivers is a weekend; a set along your daily routes is a rounding error.

Cards reward looking at the world properly — they sit on counters, shelves, dock boxes and dashboards, usually near something worth noticing. When you enter a new interior for any reason, take ten seconds to scan it like a magpie before the mission moves you on.

Track found cards against the in-game collection screen, which shows each set's gaps. Work a set's final cards as a dedicated little expedition: a set at 90% is one focused drive away from done, and finished sets are what the trophy counts.

Do not start a fourth set until three are closed. Scattered progress across six sets earns nothing; three completed sets earn the silver. Focus is the entire strategy, and the remaining sets can wait for the 100% checklist to ask for them.
trophies.tip: Choose three sets near your regular routes and finish them before touching a fourth.

trophies.name: You WAiNKer!
strategy: One hundred locations want the WAiNK treatment, and like all the silver counters this one is a marathon disguised as a joke. The locations are scattered state-wide, so the counter belongs to the hunt rules: start it on day one and feed it constantly.

Learn to recognise a WAiNK spot on sight — the branding and furniture repeat, and after twenty you will spot new ones from the road at speed. That recognition, more than any route, is what turns 100 from a grind into a habit.

Never pass a spot for later. The detour costs a minute now; the dedicated return trip costs ten. This single discipline — do it when you see it — is responsible for most of the difference between hunters who find this silver easy and hunters who find it endless.

Sweep in regions when you travel: a trip to the Keys for a strand can carry five or six spots if you drive it with your eyes open, and the stats screen's counter tells you after each session whether the habit is keeping pace with the game.

For the final twenty, work the map district by district with the counter open beside you. Endgame WAiNK spots hide in the districts the story rushed you through — the industrial edges, the swamp towns — and a methodical final sweep closes the silver without drama.
trophies.tip: Never drive past a WAiNK spot — the one-minute detour now saves a ten-minute trip later.

trophies.name: One Last Thing
strategy: Fifty challenges sounds like the grind phase's worst line until you see how the game counts: challenges are the small, specific feats scattered through its systems — driving, combat, exploration, economy — and you will complete many without ever knowing they existed.

Open the challenges screen early and read it like a menu rather than a sentence. Pin the two or three challenges closest to completion and let ordinary play finish them; the counter climbs fastest when it is aimed at nearly-done things.

Rotate categories deliberately. A session of racing feeds driving challenges, a robbery evening feeds combat and economy ones, and a strand sweep feeds exploration — variety is not a break from this trophy, it is the method of earning it.

Beware challenges with quiet prerequisites: some only start counting after a related system is unlocked or a first tier is completed. If a feat you have definitely performed shows zero progress, check whether its challenge needed activating or unlocking first.

The last handful will be specific — one vehicle class, one weapon family, one corner of the map. By then the screen names exactly what is missing, and fifty arrives as a series of small, satisfying errands rather than a single wall of work.
trophies.tip: Pin the nearly-finished challenges and let ordinary play complete them in rotation.

trophies.name: Hot Together
trophies.description: Lose a 4 star Wanted Level with your partner and escape the heat.
strategy: The setup is the trophy: both protagonists together, a genuine four-star wanted level earned while partnered, and then a clean escape where the heat fully dies. Do it inside the partner session from Phase 6, with both characters already in the same district.

Raise the level deliberately somewhere with exits — near a causeway, a swamp track or a rail line — rather than wherever chaos finds you. Four stars arrive quickly with sustained noise; what matters is that your escape route was chosen before the first star appeared.

Once at four stars, stop feeding it. Every new crime refreshes police attention and resets their search; the escape clock only runs when you are unseen, so the moment you break line of sight, become boring: change vehicle or direction once, then hide somewhere dull.

Stay together through the escape. The trophy wants the heat lost with your partner, so resist splitting up to double your chances — a partner left behind in the search zone can keep the encounter alive and void an otherwise perfect getaway.

When the last star blinks out with both of you clear, the bronze pays. If it does not, the usual causes are a wanted level that peaked at three, or a partner who was not properly grouped when the escape completed — regroup, rebuild to four, and run it again.
trophies.tip: Earn four stars near a chosen exit, break sight once, then hide somewhere boring — together.

trophies.name: Retail Therapy
trophies.description: Rob 3 shops back-to-back with your partner without losing your Wanted Level.
strategy: Three shops, back-to-back, partner present, and the wanted level must never fully die between them — this is the partner phase's real exam, and it is won on the map before it is won in the shops. Choose your three targets before you rob the first.

Pick a tight triangle of shops in one district, ideally along one road with a car parked outside the first. Travel time is the enemy: the wanted level cools while you drive, so the three robberies must chain like verses of one song, not three separate outings.

Keep each robbery short and identical: in, till, out, gone. Do not chase extra cash, do not fight the street, and do not stop to admire the work — the chain cares about continuity of heat, and every loitering second spends the wanted level you are trying to keep.

Between shops, stay visible just enough. If the stars are about to expire, a minor offence in view of a patrol refreshes them safely; what you must never do is hide so well that the level dies, because a dead level between shops breaks the chain and the count restarts.

After the third till, drop the discipline and escape properly — break sight, swap cars, cool down — and the trophy pays on the completed chain. Most failed attempts die at shop two's drive, so rehearse the triangle once clean before running it for real.
trophies.tip: Rehearse a tight triangle of three shops first — the drive between them is where chains die.

trophies.name: Whip It Good
strategy: A vehicle is discovered the first time you get in and drive it, and Leonida's traffic is a rolling showroom: one hundred distinct models is a big number that ordinary varied play quietly assembles if you refuse to drive the same favourite everywhere.

Make variety a habit from Chapter 1. Steal the interesting thing at the kerb, drive it to your destination, and let the counter grow; ten seconds of curiosity per trip outperforms an hour of dedicated car-hunting at the end of the game.

Hunt by habitat when the counter slows. Vehicle pools are regional and social: work trucks near Ambrosia's fields, boats' tow vehicles at the marinas, beaters in the swamp towns, exotics on Ocean Beach at night — a model missing from your list is usually just living somewhere you seldom go.

Car parks, dealerships and impound lots are discovery buffets. A slow lap of a big lot, hopping seat to seat, can bank a dozen models in minutes, and registering favourites to Scooter Bros at the same time feeds On the Spot as a free bonus.

Check the stats screen for the count and let the last few come from story and strand missions, which hand you unusual vehicles under controlled conditions. If a truly rare model resists, it will appear in traffic eventually — rarity in this series is a schedule, not a lock.
trophies.tip: Drive something different every trip — discovery is a habit, not a hunt.

trophies.name: Gunslinger
trophies.description: Take down 5 enemies in a single use of Combat Focus.
strategy: One activation of Combat Focus, five takedowns inside it — the trophy is a stage-management problem disguised as a shooting test. The ability's window is fixed, so the five enemies must be gathered, weakened or lined up before you ever press the button.

Choose a crowd you control: a gang operation's yard, a robbery gone loud, any fight where five or more enemies share one space. Thin the herd's edges first without Focus, and stop when exactly a roomful remains in easy reach of each other.

Position before you pop it. Stand where all five targets are visible without a camera swing across the map — a doorway, a counter, a car bonnet — because Focus time spent turning is Focus time not spent shooting, and the window does not forgive tourism.

Work nearest to farthest with the fastest reliable weapon you own, one burst per target, no double-taps out of habit. Five takedowns need five decisions, not fifty bullets, and the ability's slowdown exists precisely to make each decision deliberate.

If a run ends at four, do not chase the fifth as Focus fades — reset the stage instead. Let the fight cool, gather a fresh crowd, and run the whole setup again; this trophy falls to rehearsal within a few attempts once the staging is right.
trophies.tip: Gather five enemies in one view first — the Focus window is for shooting, not searching.

trophies.name: Catch Me If You Can
trophies.description: Make an unscheduled departure at VCIA.
strategy: VCIA — Vice City International Airport — does not approve of your travel plans: an unscheduled departure means taking a plane that was never yours, from the airport, and getting airborne. You toured this ground during VCIA Takedown; now you misuse it.

Scout in daylight first. Find where aircraft sit accessible — parked jets and props near the aprons and hangars — and note the gates and fence gaps that lead to them, because the attempt itself will be too busy for map-reading.

Arrive with modest heat or none. The departure is the crime; you do not need a wanted level as a starting condition, and beginning clean means the response is still organising itself while you are already rolling down the taxiway.

Once aboard, commit: taxi briskly, ignore the first shouts and vehicles, and take the longest straight the apron offers. Aircraft in this series forgive rough handling at low speed and punish hesitation near obstacles, so smooth and early beats fast and late.

The trophy registers as the departure counts — wheels up, airport behind you. Land somewhere quiet or simply enjoy the flight and ditch the heat in the air; either way you have turned the story's airport tour into the combat phase's easiest bronze.
trophies.tip: Scout the parked aircraft in daylight, then commit — smooth and early beats fast and late.

trophies.name: Challenging Tank
strategy: The description is the instruction, in the series' traditional wink: a Rhino is a tank, and this trophy wants you in one, making it hot — which in practice means acquiring a tank and using it until the game acknowledges your afternoon.

Tanks live where the military keeps them: bases, convoys and the heavy response that arrives when a wanted level climbs high enough in the right places. The reliable route is to provoke a serious response somewhere a Rhino can reach you, then take it from its crew.

Getting in is the dangerous minute. Approach the tank when its crew is distracted or dismounted, and expect company — bring armour, health and a fast car for the approach, because on foot in the open is exactly where a tank wants you.

Once it is yours, do what the trophy hints: make it hot. Roll somewhere the authorities care about and use the cannon until the acknowledgement lands — Rhinos are near-indestructible at first, so your real limit is boredom, not damage.

Afterwards, abandon it somewhere memorable and escape on foot or by a waiting car while the response stares at the empty tank. Few trophies on this list are as honest about being an excuse, and few set pieces are this much fun to earn.
trophies.tip: Provoke a heavy response, take the Rhino from its crew, and make it hot somewhere public.

trophies.name: Sneakthief
trophies.description: Rob a jewelry store without being detected.
strategy: No alarms, no witnesses, no wanted level: rob a jewelry store as if you were never there. This is the combat phase's stealth exam, and every part of it — timing, entry, exit — rewards the player who visits the target twice before touching it once.

Case the store in daylight as a customer. Learn the counter layout, the staff positions, the cameras' cones and the back door's habits. Jewelry stores sit in Vice City's retail districts, and the quiet hours at opening or near closing thin the witnesses to almost none.

Enter when the street is empty and the staff is fewest, and keep the weapon holstered until the moment it is needed — detection in this series is a chain of small notices, and a calm figure browsing buys seconds that a drawn gun spends instantly.

Work fast and leave faster, by the route you cased, in an unremarkable car parked a street away. The robbery only stays undetected if the exit is as invisible as the entry; a supercar idling outside is a signature, not a getaway.

If detection happens, walk away from the attempt rather than forcing it — leave, let the store reset, and run the cased plan again on a quieter hour. The trophy pays on the clean completion, and clean completions are rehearsed, never improvised.
trophies.tip: Case it twice, enter at the quiet hour, and park the getaway a street away, unremarkable.

trophies.name: Maximum Withdrawal
strategy: Five bank vaults, five escapes — the silver is The Cartel Heist with the training wheels off, repeated across Leonida's banking map. Each vault is a small heist: case it, crack it, get out, lose the heat. The count is five completions, not five attempts.

Standardise your method until it is boring: scout in daylight, note the vault's approach and the block's exits, park a fast car facing out, work the vault quickly, and drive the rehearsed route into somewhere the stars cannot follow — swamp, causeway, rail cutting.

Vary your banks. Repeating the same branch invites heavier responses and, more practically, boredom errors; five different vaults across the state also spread the travel through districts where strands, spots and cards are still waiting for you.

Escape is a skill with a rhythm: break line of sight early, change direction once while unseen, swap vehicles if the first is described on the radio, then sit somewhere dull until the level dies. A vault only counts when the escape completes, so the dull minute is part of the robbery.

Keep a written tally — bank, district, done — because five similar jobs blur together across a week. When the fifth escape cools and the silver lands, you will notice the whole combat phase has become easier: this trophy is its training montage.
trophies.tip: One rehearsed method, five different banks — and the escape is part of the robbery.

trophies.name: A Classic Blitz Play
trophies.description: Rob an Armored Truck and escape.
strategy: Armored trucks patrol Leonida's money routes on their own schedules, and the classic play is older than the series' 3D era: stop the truck, crack it open, take the money, and be gone before the response organises. One clean job earns the bronze.

Find your truck by listening to your own play first — they cross your path during ordinary driving more often than dedicated hunting suggests. When one appears and the moment suits, take the opportunity; when it does not, note its route and come back prepared.

Stop it somewhere that favours you: a quiet stretch, a junction you can block, anywhere the crew's escape and the response's arrival are both awkward. The rear doors are the target — force them with damage or explosives as the game allows, and work quickly once they open.

Grab and go. The money is the objective; a firefight with arriving units is how a thirty-second robbery becomes a ten-minute siege. Your getaway car should be yours, fast and facing the way out before the truck ever stops.

Lose the heat with the standard rhythm — break sight, change direction, swap or hide — and the trophy pays when the escape completes. It is called a classic because it is one: series veterans have been running this exact play for decades.
trophies.tip: Stop the truck somewhere awkward for everyone else, crack the rear doors, grab and go.

trophies.name: The Goodtime State
strategy: The map reveals itself where you have actually been, and this trophy wants no grey left: every district of Leonida — city, Keys, swamp, mountain and coast — visited closely enough for the map to admit it. It is the exploration phase's umbrella trophy.

Work the grey, not the map's beauty. Open the map after each phase and look for unrevealed patches; they cluster predictably — the Grassrivers' watery interior, Kalaga's far slopes, the Keys' smaller islands, the industrial edges the story never visits.

Travel by surface and vary it: roads reveal their corridors, but water reveals the coasts and swamps that roads skip, and a boat lap of the Keys plus a swamp run in an airboat-style craft will clear grey that driving never touches. Aircraft reveal fastest of all where they are available.

Fold the sweep into other work. Exploration grey sits exactly where meditation spots, WAiNK locations, stunt ramps and strand finales also hide, so a reveal-driven route planned once pays into half the guide at the same time.

When the map looks complete but the trophy has not landed, zoom in: the last grey is usually a small island, a reservoir, a single swamp channel. One deliberate afternoon with the map open beside you, hunting grey pixel by grey pixel, finishes the Goodtime State.
trophies.tip: Hunt the grey patches by boat and air as well as road — water hides half the map.

trophies.name: Pest Control
trophies.description: Rob an Illegal Operation belonging to each gang.
strategy: Every gang in Leonida runs illegal operations — stash houses, chop shops, labs, yards — and this trophy wants one robbed from each gang, not five robbed from the gang you dislike most. The work is a census as much as a crime spree.

First, learn the gangs. The story and strands introduce each crew's colours, territory and business; keep a list of gangs met, because the trophy's hidden difficulty is knowing whether the operation you just robbed was a new gang's or an old one's.

Find operations by patrolling each gang's home district with your eyes open: guarded yards, busy warehouses at odd hours, properties the map does not label but the street clearly respects. Series precedent says the game also surfaces them through tips and strand contacts as you play.

Rob each operation with the standard method — scout, park the exit car, work fast, leave by the rehearsed route — but expect the defence to reflect the owner. A lab's guards and a chop shop's are different problems wearing the same shape, so case each one fresh.

Keep the gang tally written down: gang, district, done. When every named gang has been robbed once, the trophy pays. If you reach the end unsure about one gang, the story's cast list is your checklist — an unrobbed gang is one whose operation district you have not swept.
trophies.tip: Keep a written gang tally — one operation each, and the census is the hard part.

trophies.name: In The Beginning…
trophies.description: Enjoy a cocktail with a view on Ocean Beach.
strategy: The most relaxed bronze in Leonida: go to Ocean Beach, the postcard strip of Vice City seafront, find the spot where a cocktail can be enjoyed with a view, and enjoy one. The ellipsis in the title is the series tipping its hat to where this all began.

Ocean Beach is the beachfront district along the city's east shore, thick with hotels, bars and terraces. The cocktail spot is a specific venue interaction rather than any drink anywhere, so look for the prompt where the view is the point — a terrace or rooftop facing the water.

Chapter 3's story business brings you to this neighbourhood anyway, which makes this the classic two-minute detour: finish the mission, walk to the water, and take the trophy while the city is already around you.

If the prompt does not appear, vary the hour. Some venue interactions keep venue hours, and a terrace that is shuttered at dawn is pouring by sunset; return in the evening, when Ocean Beach is lit the way the postcards promise, and try again.

Drink, view, trophy. There is no second step to optimise — except perhaps staying for the sunset, because a platinum hunt that never stops to look at Vice City has missed the point of the place entirely.
trophies.tip: Ocean Beach, evening, the terrace with the view — the prompt is the whole trophy.

trophies.name: Capital Offense
trophies.description: Smash your way out of a vehicle showroom in classic style.
strategy: A vehicle showroom, a plate-glass front, and you inside a car that needs to leave through it — the description is a scene every series veteran can already see. The trophy wants the exit done in classic style: through the glass, in the showroom's own stock.

Choose your showroom during ordinary travel: dealerships with big glass fronts and display cars inside sit in the city's retail districts. Walk in on foot first and look around like a customer — note which display car faces the glass and how much run-up it has.

Get in the display car and let the moment build properly. You are not stealing it out the back like a professional; the trophy is explicitly about style, so line up on the glass, give it a breath, and go through the window the way the scene demands.

Expect the alarm and a wanted level as your receipt. Have the next two turns planned before you move — the showroom's street, the first corner, the quiet road after — because a stylish exit followed by a clumsy arrest pleases nobody, least of all the trophy list.

Lose the heat with the standard rhythm and the bronze is yours. If the first attempt somehow fails to register, the showroom restocks and the glass is replaced — the classics are always available for another performance.
trophies.tip: Display car, plate glass, full commitment — then two planned turns and a quiet cooldown.

trophies.name: Let’s Go Bowling
trophies.description: Follow-through at the Kolt & Associates' bowling alley.
strategy: Somewhere in Leonida, Kolt & Associates keep a bowling alley, and this trophy — named for the series' most persistent invitation — asks for a follow-through there: go bowling at that alley and complete the game the alley offers.

Find the alley during your Master of None lap, since bowling is one of the activity types and the lap will take you past it. Kolt & Associates' branding marks the venue; once found, its icon joins your map for good.

Play a full game rather than a single frame. Activity trophies in this list distinguish trying from completing where the description says so, and a follow-through implies the whole motion — a complete game at the alley is the safe interpretation and costs twenty minutes at most.

Learn the alley's throwing model in the first frames: the swing timing, the drift on the lane, where your character's release point sits. Bowling systems in this series are gentle, and a strike or two usually arrives once you stop fighting the timing and repeat one calm motion.

Finish the game, take the trophy, and enjoy the small ceremony of it — of all the activities on the list, this is the one the series' fans have been being invited to for nearly twenty years. It would be rude to rush it.
trophies.tip: Find the Kolt & Associates alley on your activity lap and play one full, calm game.

trophies.name: Personal Best
strategy: The vaguest description in the partner set resolves to the simplest idea: this trophy celebrates the partnership itself — Lucia and Jason together, out in the world, doing what they do. It is earned by playing as a pair, in company, rather than by one scripted trick.

Schedule it inside the Phase 6 partner session, where both protagonists are already together for Hot Together and Retail Therapy. Most hunters find this bronze lands somewhere inside that session without being hunted at all, as a by-product of togetherness done properly.

Maximise togetherness in the meantime: travel as a pair between objectives, take partner activities when offered, and let the two share drives and downtime rather than swapping to solo play at every opportunity. The game notices the partnership it built.

If the session ends without it, review what the pair has not yet done together — the untried shared activity, the drive not taken — rather than repeating what they have. Vague trophies in this series usually hide a simple togetherness counter with one category still empty.

When it pops — often mid-drive, mid-errand, unannounced — tick it with satisfaction. Personal Best is the list's reminder that the partnership is the game's subject, and the trophy was the two of them, being them, all along.
trophies.tip: Play the partner session as a genuine pair — this one lands as a by-product of togetherness.

trophies.name: Actions Speak Louder
strategy: MISSABLE — handle with the save discipline from the rules. Somewhere in the story, a choice is offered whose outcomes matter to this trophy: it records that a real choice was made, for better or worse, and the moment does not come back around on the same save.

Your protection is already in place if you followed the roadmap: a manual save at every chapter break, in its own slot, never overwritten. Before any story sequence that smells like a point of no return — a gathering cast, a heavy conversation — add one more save on instinct.

When the choice arrives, make it as the player, not the hunter: pick the outcome that fits your Lucia and Jason. The trophy honours the choosing, and with a save behind you the other outcome remains reachable, so there is no wrong answer to agonise over.

If you finish the story and this trophy is missing, do not start a new game in anger. Reload the chapter-break save nearest before the choice, play forward to it, choose, and let the trophy register — the save system exists precisely so this costs an evening at most, not a playthrough.

After it lands either way, restore your main save if you detoured, and note in the tracker which outcome your canon carries. Choices made, trophy banked, and the hunt's most fragile bronze is safely behind you.
trophies.tip: MISSABLE: keep chapter-break saves and the choice can never cost you a playthrough.

trophies.name: Bad Luck, I Guess
strategy: MISSABLE — the list's smallest trap. The description gives the shape away: something must be failed first and then succeeded — second time's the charm — and if you succeed the first time, flawlessly, the moment passes and the trophy with it.

Your insurance is the same as the other missable's: chapter-break saves, kept religiously, plus a fresh manual save whenever a story sequence introduces a one-off test the game seems to be scoring. One-off moments announce themselves by their staging.

When you recognise the moment — a single attempt at something, with success and failure both plausible — do not play it perfectly out of pride. The trophy wants the honest sequence: an attempt that fails, then the attempt that succeeds, with the game registering both.

If you are unsure whether a failure counted, check before moving on: the attempt must genuinely fail and continue to the retry the game offers. Deliberately failing in a way that ends the sequence entirely is not the pattern the trophy is counting.

Already succeeded first try and missed it? Reload the save from before the moment, fail once on purpose, succeed on the retry, and the bronze is yours in under half an hour. This is why the saves exist — the two missables are only expensive for hunters who never made them.
trophies.tip: MISSABLE: fail the one-off moment once, then succeed — and keep a save before it.

trophies.name: The Truth Is Out There
strategy: Every game in this series keeps one weird secret — something in the sky, the swamp or the small hours that the story never explains — and this trophy, question and all, is Leonida's. The truth is out there; specifically, it is out in the state's strange corners at strange hours.

Follow the series' grammar for its mysteries: they favour remote places (the Grassrivers at night, Kalaga's heights, the far Keys), late hours, and weather with mood. If a location feels like the game is daring you to visit it at 3 a.m., it is.

Collect the rumours the game plants. Strangers, radio chatter, graffiti and odd props in this series are rarely decoration where the unexplained is concerned — when the world keeps glancing at the same phenomenon, go and stand where the glances point.

When you find the trigger, stay for the whole event. These set pieces play out in stages, and the trophy registers on the witnessing, not the arriving; leaving early because nothing has happened yet is the classic way to stand in the right place and earn nothing.

Afterwards the game will offer no explanation, which is correct. Tick the trophy, keep the location out of your strand routes if it unsettled you, and know that you have found the one bronze the developers hid for the hunters who explore like believers.
trophies.tip: Remote place, late hour, strange rumours — then stay and witness the whole event.

trophies.name: Ten Pin
trophies.description: Bowl 'em over with a melee drive-by.
strategy: A melee drive-by is exactly what it sounds like: from a moving vehicle, with a melee weapon, striking pedestrians as you pass — and ten of them, like pins, is the trophy's magic number. It is the combat list's piece of slapstick, and it wants a crowd and a kerb.

Set the stage where pedestrians gather in lines: beachfront promenades, boardwalks, bus stops, the pavement outside venues at closing time. A straight, slow street with a thick kerb crowd is a bowling lane; find one before you start swinging.

Choose reach and a steady vehicle. A bat-class weapon from a car window at moderate speed gives the widest, most forgiving arc; too fast and you pass between targets, too slow and the crowd scatters and the police arrive before the pins do.

Drive the lane in passes rather than circling wildly. One clean pass down the kerb, turn at the end, one pass back — rhythm keeps the crowd re-forming and keeps your wanted level at the merely-interested stage until the count is nearly home.

When the tenth pin falls the trophy pays; escape the modest heat with the usual rhythm and, if the count stalls, change venue rather than speed. Ten Pin falls to the right pavement far more than to the right arm.
trophies.tip: Find a crowded promenade, drive it in calm passes, and let the kerb do the arranging.

trophies.name: Dime on the Dollar
trophies.description: Earn $250,000 laundering Marked Bills through your contacts.
strategy: Marked Bills enter your life dirty — through robberies, Randy-style jobs and the story's money chapters — and leave it clean through your laundering contacts, at a rate that makes the quarter-million a marathon of bookkeeping rather than a single big score.

Build the pipeline early. The moment the game introduces a laundering contact in Chapter 2's economy, use them for every batch of Marked Bills you hold; bills hoarded in a drawer earn nothing, and the counter only counts money that has completed the wash.

Keep the supply side fed with bill-generating work you already do: bank vaults, armored trucks, gang operations and shop chains all pay partly in Marked Bills. The combat phase and this counter are the same hours spent once, if you launder after every job.

Know your contacts' capacities and cooldowns. Laundering in this kind of system usually moves money in limited batches per visit or per day, so small regular washes beat one heroic queue — drop by a contact whenever you pass one with bills in hand.

Check the laundered total on the stats screen, not your wallet: the counter is cumulative earnings through contacts, and spending the clean money afterwards does not subtract from it. At $250,000 washed, the bronze pays — a dime at a time, exactly as advertised.
trophies.tip: Launder every batch the day you earn it — the pipeline, not any single score, reaches $250k.

trophies.name: Treat Yo Self
strategy: One hundred thousand dollars spent across all shops — clothing, weapons, vehicles, everything the game's tills accept. It is the only trophy on the list that asks you to be less careful with money, and it completes itself inside an ordinary playthrough.

Do not grind it early. The hunt's economy has a real claim on your cash — garage properties for Little Boxes are expensive — so let Treat Yo Self accumulate from purchases you actually want, and only force the remainder once the garages are secure.

Spending that serves two masters is best: weapon upgrades you will use in the combat phase, vehicles that feed discovery, outfits for both protagonists. Every dollar can serve the hunt anyway; only the last few thousand are pure indulgence.

Watch the counter on the stats screen when it nears the line. If you reach the endgame a little short, the pleasant finale is a shopping trip through Vice City's best districts with both protagonists — the game has been training you for this montage since the first boutique.

When the hundredth thousand leaves your hands the trophy lands. If it somehow has not, check that your spending was in shops — services and properties may count differently from retail — and finish the difference where the clothes are expensive and the lighting is kind.
trophies.tip: Let it accumulate from purchases the hunt needs anyway; force only the final remainder.

trophies.name: Little Boxes
strategy: All the boxes, all in a row: every garage property on Leonida's market, bought and owned. The trophy is a capital project, not a skill test — its strategy is an income strategy, paced across the whole game so the final purchase never requires a desperate grind.

Map the market early. Garages appear for sale as districts open; note each one's price when you pass its sign, and keep a running total of the full set. Knowing the whole bill from Chapter 3 onwards turns saving from a hope into a plan.

Fund it with the hunt's own economy: heist takes, robbery chains, race winnings and laundered money all flow through the same wallet. Resist the two great leaks — repeated supercar purchases and restocking after careless deaths — and the property fund grows on its own.

Buy in the order the map gives them to you, cheapest detours first, rather than saving for a single spree. Owned garages are useful immediately — storage, safety, a place to keep the collection your discovery habit keeps acquiring — so each purchase pays rent in convenience.

The final garage usually waits on the endgame's bigger scores, which is by design. When the last sign flips to owned and every box on the property list is ticked, the trophy pays — and your vehicles finally all have somewhere to sleep.
trophies.tip: Price the whole set early and let the hunt's income fund it — buy as you go, cheapest first.

trophies.name: On the Spot
trophies.description: Register 10 vehicles to the Scooter Bros app.
strategy: The Scooter Bros app is Leonida's vehicle-registration service, and ten registrations is all it asks — a bronze designed to teach you a system the rest of the hunt uses constantly, since registered vehicles are the ones you can summon, store and rely on.

Register as you discover. Every time Whip It Good's habit puts you in a new vehicle you like, take the ten seconds to register it before the moment passes; ten favourites accumulate across the story without a single dedicated trip.

If you reach mid-game short of ten, a dealership or a good car park finishes it in minutes: pick ten vehicles worth keeping — a fast car, a bike, something off-road, something armoured, and six you simply enjoy — and register the set in one session.

Choose the ten like they matter, because they do: registered vehicles become your working fleet for the combat and grind phases, the cars that arrive when called and wait where left. The trophy's real reward is the fleet, not the bronze.

When the tenth registration confirms, the trophy lands and your exploration phase has its wheels. From here to the platinum, the pattern holds: the systems the easy trophies teach are the systems the hard ones assume you mastered.
trophies.tip: Register favourites to Scooter Bros as you discover them — ten across the story, no trip needed.
